title: The J-space as a union of k-sparse cones
takeaway: The equation defines the J-space as $\mathcal{F}$, the union over every size-$k$ subset of J-lens vectors of the cone of their nonnegative combinations. Because the J-lens vectors are overcomplete and would otherwise span the whole residual stream, the sparsity limit $k$ is what makes the definition pick out anything at all; the price is that the resulting object is a union of cones rather than a linear subspace.
walkthrough:
This one line is the paper's answer to a question its earlier sections leave open: what kind of mathematical object the [[j-space]] actually is.

The ingredients come from the lens. At each layer, the [[jacobian-lens]] supplies one [[j-lens-vector]] per token in the model's [[tokenizer-vocabulary]] — here written $v_1, \dots, v_n$, with $n = n_{\text{vocab}}$. Each vector is a direction in the $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional [[residual-stream]] space, and there are more vectors than dimensions. The set is overcomplete.

Overcompleteness has a consequence the paper states plainly. The vectors typically span the entire residual stream, so any activation can be written as some linear combination of them. A set that reaches everything singles out nothing. Spanning alone therefore cannot define a workspace.

The restriction that does the work is sparsity. $k$ is the allowed number of nonzero coefficients. $S$ names one choice of which $k$ tokens may contribute, $|S| = k$ fixes its size, and $\operatorname{span}\{v_i : i \in S\}$ is the set of combinations built from those $k$ vectors alone. The coefficients are also required to be nonnegative — the sentence introducing the equation says so, though the $\operatorname{span}$ symbol does not.

Nonnegativity is what turns each piece from a subspace into a cone. Scaling a point by a positive number keeps it inside; negating a vector leaves.

$\bigcup_{|S|=k}$ then sweeps over every size-$k$ subset, so $\mathcal{F}$ collects $\binom{n}{k}$ such cones. The union is not closed under addition: two points in $\mathcal{F}$ generally sum to a point outside it, because between them they may draw on more than $k$ vectors. That is the sense in which the J-space is not a linear subspace, and the word "space" is loose.

The vectors coupled with $k$ are what the paper calls a [[sparse-subframe]] — a frame because the vectors need not be independent, sparse because of the coefficient limit, and "sub" because under that limit they no longer reach the whole space.

Two things follow. The [[j-space-component]] of an activation becomes its nearest point in $\mathcal{F}$, located by [[sparse-decomposition]]. And one candidate workspace can be compared with another through [[j-space-distance]], rather than by comparing vector sets directly.

The paper hedges on $k$. It calls the level "somewhat arbitrary", varies it across experiments, and typically keeps it at or below 25, a figure taken from the measured [[j-space-occupancy]].

terms.definition: The object being defined: the J-space itself, written as a set of points in residual-stream space. It is a union of cones, not a linear subspace.
Set union. Here it joins together one cone for every admissible choice of $k$ vectors, so a point belongs to $\mathcal{F}$ if it lies in at least one of them.
A subset of the vocabulary indices — one particular choice of which J-lens vectors are allowed nonzero coefficients. Each distinct $S$ contributes its own cone to the union.
The size constraint on the subset: exactly $k$ indices. Written under the union symbol, it says the union runs over all subsets of that size.
The allowable number of positive coefficients in a decomposition, and equally the dimension of each cone. It is a chosen parameter, not something the model supplies.
The J-lens vector for vocabulary token $i$ at the layer in question: the residual-stream direction that, averaged over contexts, disposes the model to say that token.
The full collection of vocabulary vectors at one layer, indexed by token. In the paper's use these are the J-lens vectors, but the definition is stated for any such collection.
The number of vocabulary vectors in the collection. For the J-lens it equals $n_{\text{vocab}}$, the size of the tokenizer's vocabulary.
The set of combinations of the $k$ chosen vectors. The surrounding text specifies nonnegative coefficients, so despite the notation this is the cone they generate rather than the linear span.
The set of all nonnegative linear combinations of a fixed finite set of vectors. It is closed under positive scaling and under adding two of its own members, but not under negation.
The number of tokens in the model's vocabulary, and hence the number of J-lens vectors at each layer. The paper does not print its value for the models used.
The dimension of the residual stream, and therefore of the space the J-lens vectors live in. Smaller than $n_{\text{vocab}}$, which is what makes the set overcomplete.

More vectors than dimensions, so the vectors are linearly dependent and an activation has many possible decompositions rather than one. This is why a sparsity limit is needed before the definition says anything.
A spanning set of vectors that need not be linearly independent — the generalization of a basis used when directions overlap. The J-lens vectors form one because they are overcomplete.

The paper's name for the J-lens vectors together with the sparsity level $k$. Sparse because of the coefficient limit, and 'sub' because under that limit the set no longer reaches the whole residual stream.

For a given activation, the point of $\mathcal{F}$ nearest to it: the part of the activation expressible as a sparse nonnegative sum of J-lens vectors. The leftover difference is the non-J-space component.
One row of $W_U J_\ell$: the direction in residual-stream space associated with a single vocabulary token at layer $\ell$, obtained from the corpus-averaged Jacobian.

numbers.meaning: The sparsity level the formalization section says is typically used. The appendix writes '(we typically use $k \approx 25$)' when introducing the equation.
The bound section 2.3 puts on $k$. The section calls the choice 'somewhat arbitrary' and says the value is varied throughout the paper, so 25 is a habitual ceiling rather than a fixed setting.

Where the value of $k$ comes from. Section 4.2 measures J-space occupancy — the $K$ at which sparse decomposition stops beating a same-size random control — and finds it rises to a plateau of around 25 across the workspace layers, in the median case, varying across contexts.

Each cone is spanned by exactly $k$ vectors, so the paper calls them $k$-dimensional polyhedral cones. With $k \approx 25$, each piece of $\mathcal{F}$ is a 25-dimensional cone sitting inside a much larger residual-stream space.

The number of cones in the union: one for each size-$k$ subset of the $n$ vocabulary vectors. The paper does not state this count, but it follows from the union running over all $S$ with $|S| = k$, and it is astronomically large for a full tokenizer vocabulary.

The inequality that makes the J-lens vector set overcomplete. Section 2.3 states it directly; it is why the vectors typically span the entire residual stream and why the matrix formed by concatenating them is full-rank.

The excess share of activation variance the top-$K$ J-lens vectors explain over a same-size random control, at $K$ = median occupancy. Reported in section 4.2, it indicates that most of an activation lies outside $\mathcal{F}$, so the union of cones is a thin part of what the model represents.
